name: Green Chemistry
tagline: Sustainable synthesis and eco-friendly practices for a cleaner future.
seo_title: Green Chemistry — paper summaries, news & innovations | Chemisters
seo_description: Follow Chemisters Green Chemistry on LinkedIn and Facebook: paper summaries, news and innovations in sustainable synthesis, safer solvents, renewable feedstocks and green metrics.

definition.lead: Green chemistry designs products and processes that reduce or eliminate hazardous substances from the start, instead of cleaning up afterwards.
definition.body: Its 12 principles cover waste prevention, atom economy, safer solvents, energy efficiency, renewable feedstocks and catalysis. The core idea is simple: the best waste is the waste you never make.

branches.name: Atom economy
branches.summary: Designing reactions so most atoms end up in the product.

branches.name: Safer solvents
branches.summary: Replacing toxic solvents, or using none at all.

branches.name: Catalysis
branches.summary: Catalytic reagents instead of stoichiometric ones.
branches.example: Catalytic oxidations that replace chromium reagents.

branches.name: Renewable feedstocks
branches.summary: Making chemicals from biomass instead of oil.
branches.example: Plastics and solvents from plant sugars.

branches.name: Energy efficiency
branches.summary: Running reactions at room temperature and pressure where possible.

branches.name: Design for degradation
branches.summary: Products that break down harmlessly after use.

branches.name: Green metrics
branches.summary: Measuring how green a process really is.

branches.name: Safer chemicals
branches.summary: Designing molecules that keep their function with less toxicity.

timeline.title: Silent Spring
timeline.text: Rachel Carson's book raises public alarm about pesticides.
timeline.why: Helped start the modern environmental movement.

timeline.title: Pollution prevention
timeline.text: The United States passes the Pollution Prevention Act.
timeline.why: Shifted policy from cleanup to prevention.

timeline.title: Atom economy
timeline.text: Barry Trost introduces the concept of atom economy.
timeline.why: A new way to judge reactions beyond yield.

timeline.title: The E-factor
timeline.text: Roger Sheldon proposes measuring waste per kilogram of product.
timeline.why: Showed how much waste fine chemicals generate.

timeline.title: Green chemistry awards
timeline.text: The US Presidential Green Chemistry Challenge Awards are created.

timeline.title: The 12 principles
timeline.text: Paul Anastas and John Warner publish 'Green Chemistry: Theory and Practice'.
timeline.why: The framework the whole field now uses.

timeline.title: A dedicated journal
timeline.text: The Royal Society of Chemistry launches the journal Green Chemistry.
timeline.why: Green chemistry becomes an established research field.

timeline.title: A greener drug process
timeline.text: Pfizer's redesigned sertraline process wins a Presidential Green Chemistry award.
timeline.why: Showed green chemistry can also cut costs.

timeline.title: Metathesis
timeline.text: The Nobel committee calls olefin metathesis a great step forward for green chemistry.
timeline.why: Fewer steps, less waste, fewer hazardous reagents.

quiz.q: Who wrote the 12 principles of green chemistry?

options: Kilograms of waste per kilogram of product
quiz.explain: Lower is better; the ideal is zero.

options: The share of reactant atoms that end up in the product
quiz.explain: A reaction can have a 100% yield and still poor atom economy.

quiz.q: What is the first principle of green chemistry?
options: Prevention: it is better to avoid waste than to clean it up
Always use water as the reaction solvent
Never heat a reaction above room temperature
quiz.explain: Treating waste after it forms is the least efficient option.

quiz.q: Why prefer catalytic reagents over stoichiometric ones?
options: They are used in small amounts and regenerated, so less waste
They are always cheaper than any reagent
They add colour so reactions are easy to follow
quiz.explain: A stoichiometric reagent ends up as waste for every mole of product.

quiz.q: Why is supercritical CO₂ used to decaffeinate coffee?
options: It is a non-toxic solvent removed simply by releasing pressure
It is acidic and breaks down caffeine
It is very hot and evaporates the caffeine
It is oxygen that oxidizes the caffeine
quiz.explain: It replaces chlorinated solvents and leaves no residue.

quiz.q: Which sector typically has the highest E-factor?
quiz.explain: Many steps and purifications per kilogram of a complex molecule.

options: Products should break down into harmless substances after use
Products should be crushed after use
Products should be burned for energy
quiz.explain: Persistent chemicals accumulate in the environment.

quiz.q: Which 1962 book helped trigger the environmental movement?
quiz.explain: By Rachel Carson, about the effects of pesticides.
Fossil feedstocks took millions of years to form.

quiz.q: Which reaction type has the highest atom economy?
options: Addition reactions such as the Diels–Alder
quiz.explain: All reactant atoms end up in the product.

quiz.q: Which solvent is generally considered greener than dichloromethane?
quiz.explain: Solvent selection guides rank ethanol among the preferred solvents.
